description:
Space researcher, tech builder, and participant in the NASA International Space Apps Challenge 2026. I’m currently building an interactive web-based SPHEREx data explorer designed to turn complex astrophysical data into an intuitive "X-ray" experience for the cosmos.
My work focuses on bridging the gap between raw NASA IRSA/IPAC data—like 102 infrared wavelength bands and multi-detector array feeds—and clean, browser-native UI design. we  love buildings prototypes that make space exploration fun
summary:
SkyShift lets you browse the sky the way NASA’s SPHEREx infrared telescope sees it. It’s a single 8.9 MB HTML file with every asset and dataset inlined.

At its centre is an Aladin Lite viewer. Search a star, a nebula, coordinates or a city, and it shows you how it read what you typed before flying there — typos included.

SPHEREx works in six infrared bands, D1 to D6, from 0.75 to 5 µm, each split into 17 channels: 102 colours in all. A slider walks through them, and the interface tints itself as you climb in wavelength.

Three tools sit alongside. Blink flips between visits so motion jumps out; the baked dataset is interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS, ten real frames from August and December 2025. A spectrum panel plots brightness against wavelength, and an ice panel estimates ice along the line of sight. Their three samples are chosen to show the app failing honestly — one star too bright for most fits, one with suspiciously flat errors, and the Orion Nebula, which it flags UNRELIABLE and shows anyway.

A separate module blinks Barnard’s Star across 2MASS, AllWISE and SPHEREx, decades apart, and you watch it walk about ten arcseconds a year.

Round it out with a layers panel, a saved-discoveries log, phone AR, ambient sound and a judge-mode tour. Best is the honesty panel: real images and catalogue positions on one side; on the other, fluxes off by tens of percent, low-resolution ice estimates, and motion fits that ignore parallax.
details:
What is SkyShift?

SkyShift is an interactive sky viewer built on real data from NASA’s SPHEREx infrared space telescope. It pulls SPHEREx Level-2 images straight from NASA/IPAC’s Infrared Science Archive, lines them up on a common sky grid, and lets you flip between observations taken on different dates — the same blink comparator technique that was used to discover Pluto. Anything that moves, like the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS, shifts against the fixed background stars when you blink between images. It also shows each object’s infrared spectrum across SPHEREx’s wavelength bands and has a subtract mode that highlights exactly what changed between two visits.

Every image comes from the archive. Nothing is simulated. If a target has no real data yet, the app tells you that instead of filling the gap with something fake.

Why we built it

SPHEREx is scanning the entire sky in infrared light, but the raw telescope files aren’t easy for most people to open or explore. We wanted to change that. SkyShift makes the data accessible to anyone with a browser — students, curious people, educators — without needing any specialist software or installation. The whole app is a single self-contained file, so it even works offline in classrooms or places with unreliable internet.

What we hope it does

We want people to experience what it actually feels like to discover something moving in the sky. That blink-and-shift moment when a comet or asteroid slides against the stars is the same one professional astronomers have used for over a century. SkyShift puts that in a browser tab, backed by real NASA data.

Data and code

Images and image-search services: SPHEREx Level-2 data from NASA/IPAC IRSA (release QR2, DOI 10.26131/IRSA607). Processing pipeline: Python with NumPy, SciPy, and Astropy to download the files and resample them onto a common grid. The app itself is HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

Honest about limits

SPHEREx pixels are about 6 arcseconds across, so slow-moving objects show only small shifts between visits. Positional accuracy and proper motion measurements are limited by that resolution. We show the source and release information for every image so you always know exactly where the data came from.
